title: Trusts of land: disputes and orders for sale
subtitle: Section 15 and the fight over the family home
objectives: Explain the powers trustees of land hold under TLATA 1996 and the statutory rights of beneficiaries to occupy trust property
State the section 15 factors a court weighs on an application for sale, and identify how those factors change once a trustee in bankruptcy is the applicant
Apply sections 14-15 TLATA 1996 (and section 335A Insolvency Act 1986 where relevant) to a dispute between co-owners or between a co-owner and a creditor, and predict the likely outcome

leadingAuthorities.citation: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996, ss 11-15
leadingAuthorities.role: Statutory framework for trustees' powers, beneficiaries' occupation rights, and the factors on an application for sale
Confirms section 15 gives the court a genuinely wider discretion than the old trust-for-sale approach, even where a secured (non-bankruptcy) creditor applies
Displaces section 15 on a trustee-in-bankruptcy's application; tilts sharply towards sale after one year
Sets a narrow reading of 'exceptional circumstances' needed to postpone sale against a trustee in bankruptcy

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: These disputes rarely turn on abstract doctrine — they turn on whose life gets disrupted and by how much. Where the profile shows knowledge is solid but application is shaky, this note appears: 'You know the list of section 15 factors — this lesson is about weighing them against each other on real facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the section 15 checklist before. The test pool below is weighted towards scenario weighing: expect facts, not definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state the section 15 factors from memory before Part 3 — the rest of the lesson assumes you know the list cold.

overview.hook: A couple separate. One wants to sell the house and move on; the other wants to stay, with the kids, until they finish school. A bank, owed money by one of them, wants the house sold regardless of either of their wishes. All three are asking the same court for completely different outcomes — and the answer depends on four words in a 1996 Act: 'all the circumstances of the case'.

parts.heading: From trusts for sale to trusts of land
parts.voice: advisory — sets the statutory scene before the disputes begin
body: Before 1997, co-owned land was held on a 'trust for sale' — a legal fiction under which trustees were, in theory, obliged to sell the land, with any decision to keep it treated as a mere postponement of that duty. The Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 (TLATA) abolished this fiction for new trusts and converted existing ones into 'trusts of land', where sale is simply one option among the trustees' powers, not a default outcome.

Under section 6 TLATA, trustees of land have, for the purpose of exercising their functions, all the powers of an absolute owner — they can sell, retain, lease or mortgage the land as they see fit, subject to their fiduciary duties and to any restrictions in the trust instrument. Section 11 adds a duty (again, subject to contrary provision) to consult beneficiaries of full age and, so far as consistent with the general interest of the trust, to give effect to their wishes.

This matters immediately for any dispute: the starting point is no longer 'the land must eventually be sold' — it's 'the trustees have a genuine discretion, and the Act tells the court what to weigh if that discretion is contested'.

components.definition: The regime, introduced by TLATA 1996, under which co-owned (or otherwise trust-held) land is held by trustees with the full powers of an absolute owner, with sale treated as one available option rather than a presumed obligation.

interaction.prompt: Under TLATA 1996, is there a presumption that co-owned land held on trust must eventually be sold?
options: No — sale is simply one option among the trustees' powers, not a default outcome
Yes — the old 'trust for sale' presumption still applies to all trusts of land
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. TLATA deliberately removed the old presumption in favour of sale — trustees now hold the land with the full powers of an absolute owner, choosing among options rather than administering a duty to sell.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — that presumption is exactly what TLATA 1996 abolished. Sale is now one power among several, not the default outcome of holding land on trust.

parts.heading: Who gets to live there: sections 12 and 13
parts.voice: advisory — careful about the limits of a right that sounds more absolute than it is
body: Section 12 TLATA gives a beneficiary who is beneficially entitled to an interest in possession a right to occupy trust land, but only where the purposes of the trust include making the land available for occupation, or the trustees have decided the land should be available for occupation — and even then, the right does not arise if the land is unavailable or unsuitable for that beneficiary's occupation.

Section 13 lets trustees exclude or restrict that right of occupation — but not unreasonably, and not so as to exclude every beneficiary otherwise entitled to occupy. Where trustees restrict one beneficiary's occupation in favour of another's, section 13(6) lets them impose conditions, including compensation payments to the excluded beneficiary and outgoings obligations on the one who occupies.

In practice this is the mechanism behind a common family arrangement: one co-owner stays in the house, and the court (standing in the trustees' shoes under section 14) can require them to pay an occupation rent to the co-owner who has moved out, rather than forcing an immediate sale.

components.citation: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996, s 13
components.text: Trustees may exclude or restrict the entitlement of any beneficiary otherwise entitled to occupy land under section 12, but must not exercise the power unreasonably, must not exclude the entitlement of all such beneficiaries, and (where restricting one beneficiary in favour of another) may impose conditions, including compensation to the excluded beneficiary and outgoings obligations on the beneficiary in occupation.
elements: Power to exclude or restrict a s12 right of occupation
Conditions may include compensation and outgoings obligations

interaction.prompt: Section 13 TLATA lets trustees restrict a beneficiary's right to occupy trust land. Which statement correctly reflects its limits?
options: Trustees may restrict occupation as they wish, with no limit, provided a majority of trustees agree
Trustees may not exercise the power so as to exclude any beneficiary's occupation unreasonably, or exclude all beneficiaries otherwise entitled to occupy
Once one beneficiary is in occupation, section 13 prevents that beneficiary ever being excluded
interaction.explanation: Section 13 is a power to manage competing occupation rights, not an unlimited one: it cannot be used unreasonably, and it cannot strip every entitled beneficiary of the right to occupy at once.

parts.heading: Asking the court to sell: the section 15 factors
parts.voice: balancing — weighs each factor against the others before showing how outcomes tip
body: When co-owners can't agree, section 14 lets any trustee or beneficiary apply to the court for an order — including an order for sale. Section 15(1) lists the factors the court must consider: (a) the intentions of the person or persons who created the trust; (b) the purposes for which the property is held; (c) the welfare of any minor who occupies the land as their home; and (d) the interests of any secured creditor of a beneficiary. Where beneficiaries themselves are in dispute, section 15(3) adds their circumstances and wishes.

Mortgage Corp v Shaire marks the real shift here. A bank held a charge over a house co-owned by a couple (one of whose signature on an earlier charge was forged, reducing the bank's security to one beneficial share) and sought an order for sale to realise its debt. Under the old trust-for-sale approach, a secured creditor's application would very often have led to sale almost automatically. The court instead applied the section 15 factors afresh, weighed the purpose of the trust — a family home, still serving that purpose — against the practical alternative of letting the occupying co-owner pay the bank interest on the debt over time, and refused an immediate order for sale.

The lesson from Shaire isn't that creditors always lose — it's that section 15 genuinely widened the court's discretion compared with the pre-1996 law, and a court is now required to give real weight to the purpose the property still serves, not just to the fact that a creditor wants to be paid.

components.label: The section 15(1) factors
points: (a) The intentions of the person(s) who created the trust
(b) The purposes for which the property is held
(c) The welfare of any minor who occupies the land as their home
(d) The interests of any secured creditor of a beneficiary
Where beneficiaries dispute among themselves, s15(3) adds their own circumstances and wishes

components.factsShort: A bank's charge, taken after a forged signature, secured only one co-owner's beneficial share of a family home still occupied by the other co-owner. The bank sought an order for sale.
components.ratioShort: Section 15 requires the court to weigh the purpose the property still serves against the creditor's interest afresh — sale is not the default outcome once a secured creditor applies.

expanded.facts: Mr Shaire had forged his wife's signature on a further charge over their jointly owned home. The mortgage corporation's security was therefore confined to Mr Shaire's own beneficial share. Mrs Shaire remained living in the property, which continued to serve as her home. The bank applied under section 14 TLATA for an order for sale to realise its debt.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court held that section 15 replaced the old trust-for-sale presumption with a genuinely open weighing exercise. It considered the purpose for which the property was held (a family home, a purpose that continued), the practical alternative of Mrs Shaire servicing interest on the debt rather than losing her home immediately, and the bank's interest in eventually being paid, and declined to order immediate sale.
expanded.significance: Shaire is the clearest illustration that TLATA's section 15 factors are not just a restatement of the old law dressed in new language — they give the court real room to protect a property's continuing purpose as a home even against a secured, non-bankruptcy creditor.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is a court most likely to follow the Shaire approach and decline an immediate order for sale?
interaction.scenarioA: A commercial lender holds a charge over a buy-to-let property that has never been anyone's home, and the mortgagor is in arrears with no realistic prospect of repayment.
interaction.scenarioB: A bank holds a charge over the family home following a forged signature on the charge; the house is still occupied by the non-signing co-owner as her home, and she can service interest on the debt from her own income.
interaction.explanation: Shaire turned on the property still serving its purpose as a home and a realistic alternative to immediate sale being available. Scenario A has neither: no home purpose to protect, and no realistic prospect of servicing the debt another way.

parts.heading: When a trustee in bankruptcy knocks: section 335A
parts.voice: balancing, but honest about how far the balance tips after bankruptcy
body: Everything changes once one co-owner is made bankrupt. Their beneficial share vests in a trustee in bankruptcy, whose job is to realise assets for creditors — and an application for sale by a trustee in bankruptcy is governed not by section 15 TLATA at all, but by section 335A Insolvency Act 1986, a separate and much less forgiving test.

Section 335A(2) directs the court to consider: the interests of the bankrupt's creditors; where the application concerns a dwelling-house that is or has been the home of the bankrupt, their spouse or civil partner, or former spouse or civil partner, the conduct of that spouse or former spouse so far as it contributed to the bankruptcy, their needs and financial resources, and the needs of any children; and all the circumstances of the case other than the needs of the bankrupt.

Then comes the sting: section 335A(3) provides that where the application is made more than one year after the bankrupt's estate vested in the trustee, the court shall assume, unless the circumstances of the case are exceptional, that the interests of the creditors outweigh all other considerations. Re Citro shows how high that bar sits: the wives of two bankrupt brothers argued that being forced to leave the family home during their children's schooling would cause real hardship — and the Court of Appeal held that hardship of that kind, however real, is the ordinary and melancholy consequence of a spouse's bankruptcy, not an exceptional circumstance capable of postponing sale.

The practical effect is that the first year after bankruptcy is the window in which a family genuinely has room to argue for postponement. After that, only something well outside the ordinary consequences of debt — a terminal illness, for instance — has any real prospect of displacing the presumption in favour of the creditors.

components.text: On an application by a trustee in bankruptcy for an order for sale of a dwelling-house, the court has regard to the interests of the bankrupt's creditors, the conduct, needs and resources of a spouse or former spouse, the needs of any children, and all the circumstances other than the needs of the bankrupt. Where the application is made more than one year after the bankrupt's estate vested in the trustee, the court shall assume, unless the circumstances are exceptional, that the creditors' interests outweigh all other considerations.
elements: Conduct, needs and resources of a spouse or former spouse
All other circumstances except the bankrupt's own needs
After one year: presumption for creditors unless exceptional circumstances

components.factsShort: Two brothers were made bankrupt. Their estranged wives, still living in the family homes with children mid-schooling, argued that an immediate sale would cause severe hardship.
components.ratioShort: The ordinary hardship of a family losing its home on bankruptcy — disruption to children's schooling included — is not an 'exceptional circumstance' capable of postponing sale.

expanded.facts: Domenico and Carmine Citro were both made bankrupt, each with an interest in a family home occupied by his estranged wife and children. The trustees in bankruptcy applied for orders for sale. The wives resisted, pointing to the distress and practical difficulty of rehousing their families, including school-age children, on short notice.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the wives' circumstances, though genuinely difficult, were the kind of hardship that follows almost any bankruptcy involving a family home — loss of accommodation, disruption to children, financial strain. To count as exceptional, circumstances need to be outside the ordinary run of cases of this type, not merely severe within it.
expanded.significance: Re Citro remains the benchmark for how narrowly 'exceptional circumstances' is read under the modern section 335A. It is cited precisely because ordinary family hardship, however real, does not meet the bar — something has to be genuinely unusual, not just distressing.

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through them on a trustee-in-bankruptcy's application under section 335A.
items: The bankrupt's beneficial share vests in the trustee in bankruptcy
The trustee in bankruptcy applies to the court for an order for sale
The court considers the s335A(2) factors, including the needs of any children and the conduct of the spouse
If the application is made more than one year after the vesting, the court presumes creditors' interests outweigh other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: vesting first, then the application, then the section 335A(2) weighing, and only then — if more than a year has passed — the strong presumption in favour of creditors.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — vesting has to happen before the trustee can apply, and the one-year presumption only becomes relevant after the factors have been identified, not before.

parts.heading: Weighing it up: family home against creditor
parts.voice: advisory — synthesises the two regimes into a single practical checklist
body: Two different tests, two different starting points: an ordinary dispute between co-owners, or an application by a non-bankruptcy secured creditor, goes through section 15 TLATA, where the purpose of the trust and the welfare of resident children carry real weight, and Shaire shows a court can and will refuse sale where the property still serves as someone's home and the debt can be serviced another way. Bankruptcy strips almost all of that away: section 335A applies instead, and after the first year, only exceptional circumstances — not ordinary hardship — will save the home.

The examiner's favourite trap is testing whether you've noticed which regime applies. A fact pattern that mentions 'the bank obtained a charging order' is not automatically a bankruptcy case — charging orders and mortgagee applications generally stay under section 15. A fact pattern that mentions the co-owner has been 'made bankrupt' or has a 'trustee in bankruptcy' takes you straight to section 335A, and the ordinary section 15 factors about the trust's purpose become far less relevant.

Once you've identified the right test, the analysis is really just structured weighing: whose interest does the property currently serve, how urgent and genuine is the creditor's need to realise its money, and — critically in bankruptcy cases — has more or less than a year passed since the estate vested.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often apply the section 15 TLATA factors (purpose of the trust, welfare of minors) to a bankruptcy scenario, treating them as if they still governed once a trustee in bankruptcy is involved.
components.whyItsWrong: Section 335A Insolvency Act 1986 displaces section 15 entirely once the applicant is a trustee in bankruptcy. The welfare-of-children and purpose-of-trust language does not carry across; the relevant factors are the s335A(2) list, and after one year the creditors' interests are presumed to outweigh everything else bar exceptional circumstances.

interaction.prompt: Priti and Jorge are unmarried co-owners of a house where their two young children live with Priti after separation. Jorge has been made bankrupt, and 14 months after his estate vested, his trustee in bankruptcy applies for an order for sale. Priti argues the children's schooling would be badly disrupted by a move. What is the likely outcome?
options: The court applies section 15 TLATA and gives the children's welfare equal weight to the creditors' interests, likely refusing sale

The court applies section 335A Insolvency Act 1986; because more than a year has passed since vesting, it will presume the creditors' interests outweigh other considerations unless the disruption is exceptional — and ordinary schooling disruption, per Re Citro, is unlikely to meet that bar
No order for sale can be made at all because the children are minors in occupation of the home
interaction.explanation: A trustee in bankruptcy's application is governed by section 335A, not section 15. More than a year has passed since vesting, so the presumption in favour of creditors applies, and Re Citro shows that ordinary disruption to schooling does not count as exceptional.

testPool.prompt: Name the Act that replaced the 'trust for sale' with the 'trust of land' for co-owned property.
acceptableAnswers: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996
testPool.modelAnswer: The Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 (TLATA) abolished the trust for sale in favour of the trust of land, under which sale is one option among the trustees' powers rather than a default duty.

testPool.prompt: Under section 6 TLATA, do trustees of land have, for the purpose of exercising their functions, all the powers of an absolute owner?
options: Yes
No — their powers are limited to what the trust instrument expressly lists

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the section 15(1) factors a court considers on a TLATA application for sale?
options: The intentions of the person(s) who created the trust
The purposes for which the property is held
The age of the youngest trustee
The welfare of any minor who occupies the land as their home
testPool.trapExplanation: The age of a trustee has no bearing on section 15 — the factors focus on the trust's purpose, the interests of occupying minors and secured creditors, and (where beneficiaries dispute) their own circumstances, not on anything about the trustees personally.

testPool.prompt: Section 15(3) TLATA adds a further set of factors where the dispute is between beneficiaries themselves. What does it add?
options: The circumstances and wishes of beneficiaries of full age entitled to an interest in possession
The professional qualifications of the trustees
Nothing — section 15(3) simply repeats section 15(1)

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows on a mortgagee's (non-bankruptcy) application for sale under section 14 TLATA.
items: A secured creditor applies to the court under section 14 for an order for sale
The court considers the section 15(1) factors, including the purpose the property still serves
The court weighs whether the debt can realistically be serviced without an immediate sale
The court decides whether to order sale, postpone it, or attach conditions

testPool.prompt: In the passage below (paraphrasing the reasoning in Mortgage Corp v Shaire), highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The bank's charge secured only a proportion of the beneficial interest, and the property continued to serve its purpose as Mrs Shaire's home. Section 15 requires the court to weigh that purpose afresh against the creditor's interest, rather than treating sale as the default outcome once a secured creditor applies.
testPool.ratioSentence: Section 15 requires the court to weigh that purpose afresh against the creditor's interest, rather than treating sale as the default outcome once a secured creditor applies.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is governed by section 15 TLATA rather than section 335A Insolvency Act 1986?
testPool.scenarioA: A trustee in bankruptcy applies for sale of the family home three years after the bankrupt's estate vested.
testPool.scenarioB: A bank with a non-bankruptcy charging order applies for sale of the same family home, which is still occupied by the co-owner's children.
testPool.explanation: Scenario B involves an ordinary secured creditor, not a trustee in bankruptcy, so section 15 TLATA governs. Scenario A involves a trustee in bankruptcy, which takes it to section 335A Insolvency Act 1986 instead.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether the section 335A(3) presumption in favour of creditors applies.
testPool.scenarioText: Two years after Karim is made bankrupt, his trustee in bankruptcy applies for an order for sale of the house where Karim's ex-partner and their teenage daughter still live. The ex-partner argues that moving would disrupt the daughter's final year of GCSEs.
tappableSpans: disrupt the daughter's final year of GCSEs
testPool.explanation: More than a year has passed since the estate vested, so the presumption in favour of creditors' interests applies unless the circumstances are exceptional — and GCSE disruption, on Re Citro's reasoning, is unlikely to be exceptional.

testPool.prompt: A non-bankruptcy secured creditor applies for sale of a house that has been substantially adapted for the mobility needs of an elderly, disabled co-owner who still lives there and can service interest on the debt. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The court is likely to weigh the property's continuing purpose and the occupier's needs heavily under section 15, and may decline immediate sale, following the approach in Shaire
The court must order sale immediately because a secured creditor has applied
Disability is irrelevant to a section 15 application
testPool.explanation: As in Shaire, a non-bankruptcy creditor's application goes through section 15, which lets the court weigh the property's continuing purpose (here, adapted, ongoing accommodation for a vulnerable occupier) against the creditor's interest — sale is not automatic.

testPool.prompt: Two siblings co-own a buy-to-let flat, bought purely as an investment and never occupied by either of them or anyone else as a home. One wants to sell; the other refuses. What is the likely outcome on a section 14 application?
options: Sale is likely to be ordered — the trust's purpose was investment, not occupation, so there is no continuing home-purpose for the court to protect
The court must refuse sale because both siblings are beneficiaries of full age
Section 15 does not apply to investment properties at all
testPool.explanation: Where the trust's purpose (investment) is not tied to anyone's occupation, the section 15(1)(b) factor that protected the Shaire family home has nothing to bite on, so sale is far more likely to follow.

testPool.prompt: A beneficiary is excluded from occupying trust property under section 13 because another beneficiary already occupies it. Can the excluded beneficiary claim compensation?
options: Yes — trustees can impose compensation conditions on the occupying beneficiary under section 13(6)
No — section 13 never allows any form of compensation

testPool.prompt: Aisha and Ben bought a house together as an unmarried couple; the trust deed recorded it was bought 'for their joint occupation as a family home'. They separate. Ben, now bankrupt for 18 months, has his trustee in bankruptcy apply for sale. Aisha still lives there with their eight-year-old son and argues the disruption would be exceptional because the son has a diagnosed anxiety condition said to be exacerbated by house moves. Analyse whether the trustee in bankruptcy is likely to obtain an order for sale.
factsToOrder: The trust deed records the property was bought for joint occupation as a family home
Ben is bankrupt, and his trustee applies for sale 18 months after the estate vested
Aisha and the couple's eight-year-old son still occupy the property
The son has a diagnosed anxiety condition said to be exacerbated by moving house

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the trustee in bankruptcy is likely to obtain an order for sale, given more than a year has passed since vesting and Aisha resists on the basis of her son's diagnosed condition.
modelAnswer.rule: An application by a trustee in bankruptcy is governed by section 335A Insolvency Act 1986, not section 15 TLATA. After one year from vesting, the court presumes the creditors' interests outweigh all other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional. Re Citro establishes that ordinary hardship to a family, including disruption to children's schooling, does not count as exceptional.
modelAnswer.application: 18 months have passed since vesting, so the one-year presumption applies. The trust deed's stated purpose (a family home) is not, on its own, relevant under section 335A the way it would be under section 15 — that factor belongs to the wrong regime. A generalised anxiety condition, without stronger medical evidence that a move would cause harm well beyond the ordinary disruption any child experiences, sits close to the kind of hardship Re Citro treated as insufficient, though a well-evidenced, serious medical risk could in principle be argued as exceptional.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On the facts as given, sale is likely to be ordered: the presumption in favour of creditors applies, and without more compelling medical evidence, ordinary disruption to a child's life — however genuinely distressing — is unlikely to meet the high bar Re Citro sets for exceptional circumstances.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that 'the children's education will be disrupted by a house move' counts, on its own, as an exceptional circumstance under section 335A(3)?
testPool.explanation: Re Citro treats this kind of disruption as the ordinary, if regrettable, consequence of a family member's bankruptcy — not something outside the general run of such cases, which is what 'exceptional' requires.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures why Re Citro is still cited today despite predating TLATA 1996?
options: Because section 335A Insolvency Act 1986 uses materially the same 'exceptional circumstances' language the courts had already been applying, so Re Citro's narrow reading of what counts as exceptional continues to guide its interpretation
Because Re Citro was expressly overruled and now illustrates the opposite of current law
Because TLATA 1996 abolished section 335A entirely
testPool.trapExplanation: Re Citro predates TLATA, but it interprets the same 'exceptional circumstances' test that section 335A still uses today, so its narrow approach carries straight across rather than being displaced by the 1996 reforms.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the section 15 TLATA factors to a bankruptcy case, or vice versa. Identify which regime governs — is there a trustee in bankruptcy, and has more than a year passed since vesting — before you weigh anything.
